cards.title: The Do-Not-Roll-Your-Own Rule
cards.teaser: Cryptography is the one field where intelligence and effort actively work against you. The more clever your custom scheme, the more likely it harbors a subtle flaw that a trained cryptanalyst will exploit in minutes. Use vetted libraries; never invent your own primitives.

runs.text: Jean-Philippe Aumasson opens
Serious Cryptography

with a blunt observation: cryptographic algorithms are designed by teams of PhDs, attacked by other teams of PhDs over years of public scrutiny, and still sometimes broken. A developer implementing their own cipher over a weekend is not competing on an equal footing.
The rule has two layers:

items.text: Do not invent new algorithms.
XOR-ing data with a key, encoding in Base64, or combining MD5 with your own twist does not produce security. It produces an obstacle that a moderately competent attacker will walk around.
Do not implement standard algorithms from scratch.

Implementing AES from the spec is an excellent learning exercise. It is a catastrophic production choice. Timing side-channels, padding oracle vulnerabilities, and key-scheduling bugs in hand-rolled code are real, common, and hard to find in review.

runs.text: What to use instead:
libsodium
(C, with bindings for every major language) for general-purpose crypto; language-native standard libraries (Python's
cryptography
, Java's JCE, Go's
crypto/
package, Node's built-in
crypto
module) for everything else. David Wong's
Real-World Cryptography
consistently steers readers toward libsodium's opinionated API precisely because it makes misuse difficult by design.

"Security through obscurity" — hiding an algorithm rather than publishing it — is not cryptographic security. A secure algorithm must remain secure even when the attacker knows exactly how it works (Kerckhoffs's principle, 1883). If your scheme's security depends on the attacker not knowing your code, it is not secure.

Cryptography is not "hard to break"; it is mathematically provable under specific conditions. When you invent your own version, those proofs no longer apply — and you probably introduced a flaw that a trained attacker will find in minutes. Use vetted libraries and standard algorithms.

cards.title: Symmetric Encryption and AES
cards.teaser: Symmetric encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt. AES is the modern standard — fast, hardware-accelerated on virtually every platform, and unbroken at practical key sizes. Understanding key sizes and what AES actually does is the minimum context for using it correctly.

runs.text: Symmetric encryption has one defining property: the same secret key both encrypts and decrypts. This makes it fast (no expensive asymmetric math) and suitable for bulk data, but creates the key distribution problem — how do you share the key with the other party without an attacker intercepting it?

The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) is a block cipher standardized by NIST in 2001, selected from the Rijndael submission by Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen. It operates on 128-bit blocks and supports three key sizes:

items.text: AES-128
— 128-bit key, 10 rounds. Entirely adequate for most applications. The security margin is large enough that no practical attack exists.
AES-192
— 192-bit key, 12 rounds. Rarely used; offers minimal benefit over AES-128 in practice.
AES-256
— 256-bit key, 14 rounds. Required by many compliance frameworks (FIPS 140-2, NSA Suite B for top-secret data). Preferred for new systems unless performance is the bottleneck.

runs.text: Modern CPUs include AES-NI hardware instructions that execute AES operations in a single clock cycle. On any modern server or mobile CPU, AES encryption throughput exceeds 10 GB/s — performance is not a reason to choose a weaker algorithm.

AES alone is a block cipher — it encrypts exactly one 128-bit block deterministically. A bare block cipher is not an encryption scheme. You need a mode of operation (covered next) to encrypt variable-length messages securely.

AES is the standard for symmetric encryption. It takes a 128-, 192-, or 256-bit key and encrypts data in 128-bit chunks. By itself it is just a scrambling function for one block — you need a mode of operation on top of it to encrypt real messages.

cards.title: Block Cipher Modes: ECB, CBC, CTR, and GCM
cards.teaser: A block cipher mode determines how AES is applied across multiple blocks. The choice of mode is not a detail — ECB is demonstrably broken, CBC requires careful padding handling, and GCM is the modern choice that also provides authentication. The ECB penguin is the most famous illustration of why mode choice matters.

runs.text: Because AES encrypts exactly one 128-bit block, encrypting a multi-block message requires a strategy for how blocks relate to each other. That strategy is the mode of operation.

items.text: ECB (Electronic Codebook) — broken.

Each block is encrypted independently with the same key. Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks. The "ECB penguin" demonstrates this perfectly: encrypt a bitmap of a penguin with AES-ECB and the penguin's silhouette remains visible in the ciphertext because large uniform regions (sky, body) encrypt to matching blocks. ECB leaks structural information. Never use it for real data.
CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) — legacy.

Each plaintext block is XOR'd with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, preventing the ECB problem. Requires a random Initialization Vector (IV). Vulnerable to padding oracle attacks (BEAST, POODLE) when used in network protocols with CBC + padding. Acceptable for file encryption with careful implementation; avoid for new TLS/web use.
CTR (Counter Mode) — stream cipher construction.

Encrypts a counter value to produce a keystream, then XORs with plaintext. Allows parallel encryption and random access to ciphertext blocks. No padding required. Does not provide authentication — an attacker who can flip bits in ciphertext will flip the corresponding bits in decrypted plaintext without detection.
GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) — modern AEAD standard.

CTR mode plus a Galois field authentication tag. Provides encryption and authentication in one pass. Produces a 128-bit authentication tag that detects any tampering. Hardware-accelerated on the same CPUs that support AES-NI. The correct default for new code.

runs.text: AES-GCM nonce reuse is catastrophic. If you encrypt two different messages with the same key and the same nonce (IV), an attacker can recover both plaintexts and the authentication key. Nonces must be unique per (key, message) pair — use a random 96-bit nonce generated fresh for every encryption operation.

The mode controls how AES handles messages longer than one 128-bit block. ECB encrypts each block the same way — so identical blocks look identical in ciphertext, leaking structure (the penguin problem). GCM is the modern choice: it encrypts securely and produces an authentication tag that catches any tampering.

cards.title: AEAD: Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data
cards.teaser: AEAD solves a problem that pure encryption does not: it ensures that ciphertext has not been tampered with and that the associated context (headers, metadata) matches what was intended. AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are the two AEAD algorithms developers should know.

runs.text: Encryption alone provides confidentiality — a ciphertext hides the plaintext. It does
not

provide integrity. An attacker can flip bits in a CBC ciphertext and predictably corrupt or alter the decrypted output without knowing the key. Historically, this led developers to bolt on separate MACs — and to do so in the wrong order (encrypt-then-MAC vs MAC-then-encrypt vs MAC-and-encrypt, only the first being secure).

AEAD bakes authentication into the encryption scheme. It produces a single output: encrypted data plus an authentication tag. Decryption fails loudly if the tag does not verify — before any plaintext is returned. The "associated data" component lets you authenticate non-encrypted context (packet headers, user IDs, protocol version bytes) without including it in the ciphertext.

items.text: AES-GCM
— AES-CTR for encryption, GHASH for authentication. Hardware-accelerated on x86/ARM. The standard choice when AES-NI is available. Nonce must be unique (96 bits recommended, never reuse).
ChaCha20-Poly1305

— ChaCha20 stream cipher plus Poly1305 MAC. Designed by Daniel Bernstein. Faster than AES-GCM in software without hardware acceleration (mobile, IoT, lower-end CPUs). Resistant to timing attacks without hardware support. Required in TLS 1.3 alongside AES-GCM.

runs.text: In practice: use AES-256-GCM as your default; fall back to ChaCha20-Poly1305 when you need software-only performance or are targeting environments without AES-NI. Both are in TLS 1.3's mandatory cipher suite list. David Wong's
Real-World Cryptography
devotes a full chapter to AEAD and recommends these two as the only choices a developer should seriously consider.

The "associated data" in AEAD is authenticated but not encrypted. Use it for metadata that must be integrity-protected but can be read in plaintext: a user ID binding a ciphertext to an account, a protocol version byte, a timestamp. If an attacker modifies the associated data, decryption fails.

AEAD gives you encryption plus a tamper-proof seal in one step. If anyone modifies the ciphertext or the metadata attached to it, decryption fails before you ever see the plaintext. AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are the two algorithms worth knowing.

cards.title: Asymmetric Encryption: RSA and Elliptic Curve
cards.teaser: Asymmetric encryption uses two mathematically linked keys — a public key to encrypt, a private key to decrypt — solving the key distribution problem. RSA works but carries well-known failure modes; Elliptic Curve cryptography (Curve25519, secp256r1) is the modern choice for new systems.

runs.text: Asymmetric (public-key) cryptography solves the problem symmetric encryption cannot: how do two parties establish a shared secret over an untrusted channel without having met in advance? The mathematics relies on trapdoor functions — operations that are easy to compute in one direction and computationally infeasible to reverse without the secret.

items.text: RSA

— based on the difficulty of factoring large integers. Invented by Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman in 1977. RSA quirks developers must know: textbook RSA (no padding) is completely insecure; always use OAEP for encryption and PSS for signatures. Key sizes must be at least 2048 bits (3072+ for new systems); 1024-bit RSA was broken in 2010. RSA operations are significantly slower than ECC operations at equivalent security levels. A 2048-bit RSA key provides roughly the same security as a 112-bit symmetric key — considerably less than AES-128.
Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC)

— based on the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem. Much smaller key sizes for equivalent security: a 256-bit ECC key provides roughly the same security as a 3072-bit RSA key. Two curves dominate practical use:
Curve25519 (X25519 for key exchange, Ed25519 for signatures)

— designed by Daniel Bernstein with conservative security parameters, resistance to side-channel attacks, and simple implementation rules. The recommended choice for new code; used by default in libsodium, TLS 1.3, SSH.

— NIST standard curve, widely supported in browsers, TLS stacks, and HSMs. Slightly more complex to implement safely than Curve25519 but broadly interoperable. Used in ECDSA signatures throughout TLS certificate infrastructure.

runs.text: Asymmetric encryption is not a drop-in replacement for symmetric encryption. It is orders of magnitude slower and cannot encrypt arbitrary-length data directly. In practice, asymmetric operations are used to establish or exchange a symmetric key, which then encrypts actual data — this is the hybrid encryption pattern used by TLS.

Asymmetric encryption lets strangers communicate securely: you publish a public key, anyone can encrypt to you, only your private key can decrypt. RSA is old and works but has sharp edges; Elliptic Curve crypto gives stronger security with smaller, faster keys.

cards.title: Hash Functions: SHA-2, SHA-3, and What They Are Not
cards.teaser: A cryptographic hash function maps arbitrary input to a fixed-length digest with three properties: preimage resistance, second preimage resistance, and collision resistance. SHA-256 and SHA-3 are the current standards. What hash functions are NOT is just as important to understand — they are not encryption and they cannot protect passwords.

runs.text: A cryptographic hash function takes arbitrary input and produces a fixed-size output (digest) with three security properties:

items.text: Preimage resistance
— given a digest, it is computationally infeasible to find any input that produces it.
Second preimage resistance
— given an input and its digest, it is infeasible to find a different input with the same digest.
Collision resistance
— it is infeasible to find any two different inputs that produce the same digest.

runs.text: The SHA-2 family (SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512) is the current standard for general use — digital signatures, integrity checks, HMACs, certificate fingerprints. SHA-3 (Keccak) uses a different internal structure (sponge construction vs Merkle-Damgard) and is suitable where independence from SHA-2 is desired, such as post-quantum hybrid schemes.
What hash functions are
not

items.text: Not encryption.
Hashing is one-way. You cannot recover the original input from a digest.
Not password storage.
SHA-256 is fast — a GPU can compute billions per second, making brute-force attacks trivial. Password storage requires a KDF (next card).
Not MAC or authentication.
A plain hash provides no authentication; anyone can compute the hash of any message. Use HMAC.

runs.text: MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for cryptographic purposes. MD5 collisions can be computed in seconds; SHA-1 was practically broken by Google's SHAttered attack in 2017. Never use either for security-sensitive applications. Their only remaining legitimate use is checksums for accidental corruption detection (not adversarial tampering) in legacy contexts.

A hash function takes any input and produces a fixed-size fingerprint. It is one-way, deterministic, and any change to input produces a completely different fingerprint. SHA-256 is the standard. What it is not: encryption (you cannot reverse it), password storage (too fast — attackers can try billions per second), or authentication on its own (use HMAC instead).

cards.title: KDFs: PBKDF2, scrypt, and Argon2
cards.teaser: Key Derivation Functions are deliberately slow, memory-hard functions designed for deriving cryptographic keys from passwords or low-entropy secrets. Argon2id is the current best practice for password hashing; PBKDF2 is the compliance-driven fallback. Never use a raw hash function to store passwords.

runs.text: The problem with hashing passwords directly with SHA-256 is that SHA-256 is optimized for speed. An attacker with a stolen password hash database and a GPU cluster can attempt billions of SHA-256 computations per second, brute-forcing typical user passwords in minutes.
Key Derivation Functions (KDFs) address this by being deliberately expensive — tunable to require significant CPU time, memory, or both. Three matter for developers:

items.text: PBKDF2

— iterates an HMAC (typically HMAC-SHA256) thousands to hundreds of thousands of times. Widely supported; required by NIST and FIPS. CPU-bound but not memory-hard — large-scale GPU attacks remain practical even at high iteration counts. Use when FIPS compliance is mandatory; otherwise prefer Argon2.
scrypt

— adds memory-hardness on top of PBKDF2. Requires a tunable amount of RAM during computation, making GPU parallelism expensive. Designed by Colin Percival. Good choice if Argon2 is unavailable. Parameter selection (N, r, p) requires care.
Argon2id

— winner of the 2015 Password Hashing Competition. Three variants: Argon2i (side-channel resistant, suitable for KDFs in adversarial environments), Argon2d (maximum GPU resistance), Argon2id (hybrid — recommended for password hashing). Tunable memory (m), iterations (t), and parallelism (p). The current consensus recommendation from OWASP and Aumasson's
Serious Cryptography

runs.text: Always generate a unique, cryptographically random salt (16+ bytes) for each password and store it alongside the hash. The salt prevents rainbow table attacks and ensures that two users with the same password have different stored hashes.

OWASP recommended Argon2id parameters (2024): m=19456 (19 MiB), t=2, p=1. For PBKDF2 when required: 600,000 iterations with HMAC-SHA256. These numbers increase over time as hardware improves — check OWASP's current cheat sheet.

A KDF is a deliberately slow hash designed to make brute-forcing passwords expensive. Argon2id is the best current choice — it requires both CPU time and memory, making GPU attacks impractical. Never store passwords with SHA-256 or bcrypt is a distant second to Argon2.

cards.title: HMAC: Keyed Message Authentication
cards.teaser: HMAC binds a secret key to a hash computation, producing a message authentication code that only someone with the key can verify or generate. HMAC-SHA256 is the standard — it appears in TLS, JWTs, API authentication, and webhook signatures. Understanding why naive keyed hashing fails is essential context.

runs.text: A message authentication code (MAC) answers the question: "Did this specific party (who holds the key) produce this specific message, and has the message been altered?" A plain hash does not answer this — anyone can compute
SHA256(message)
without a key.
The naive approach —
SHA256(key || message)

— is vulnerable to a length extension attack when using SHA-2 (Merkle-Damgard construction). An attacker who knows the MAC but not the key can append data to the message and compute a valid MAC for the extended message. HMAC was designed specifically to close this.
HMAC uses nested hashing:

items.text: HMAC(K, m) = H((K XOR opad) || H((K XOR ipad) || m))
— the inner hash covers the key-padded message; the outer hash covers the key-padded inner result. The double-key structure prevents length extension attacks.

runs.text: Where HMAC-SHA256 appears in practice:

items.text: TLS 1.2 PRF
— derives keying material from the master secret.
JWT HS256
— signs the JWT payload with a shared secret.
Webhook signatures
— GitHub, Stripe, and Twilio sign webhook payloads with HMAC-SHA256 so recipients can verify origin and integrity.
AWS Signature Version 4
— signs API requests using a series of HMAC-SHA256 operations.

runs.text: Always use constant-time comparison when verifying HMACs. Standard string equality short-circuits on the first differing byte, leaking timing information that allows an attacker to forge MACs byte by byte. Use hmac.compare_digest() in Python, crypto.timingSafeEqual() in Node, or the equivalent in your language.

HMAC ties a secret key to a hash so only someone with the key can produce or verify the result. It is how webhook senders prove their identity, how JWTs are signed with shared secrets, and how TLS derives session keys. Always use constant-time comparison when checking it.

cards.title: Digital Signatures: RSA-PSS, ECDSA, and Ed25519
cards.teaser: A digital signature proves that the holder of a private key produced or endorsed a specific message — providing non-repudiation and authentication without a shared secret. RSA-PSS is the safe RSA signature scheme; ECDSA is standard but implementation-sensitive; Ed25519 is the clean modern choice.

runs.text: Digital signatures provide two properties that HMAC does not: they work asymmetrically (the verifier does not need the secret signing key) and they provide non-repudiation (the signer cannot later deny having signed). The private key signs; the public key verifies.

items.text: RSA-PSS (Probabilistic Signature Scheme)

— the correct way to sign with RSA. Avoids the determinism and malleability problems of the older PKCS#1 v1.5 scheme. Requires a minimum 2048-bit key (3072+ for new deployments). Slower than ECC; large signatures.
ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm)
— standard ECC signature scheme, widely used in TLS certificates and blockchain protocols. Critical implementation requirement: the nonce
k

must be unique and secret for every signature. Sony's PS3 private key was extracted because ECDSA signing reused the same nonce. Use deterministic ECDSA (RFC 6979) or a library that handles nonce generation for you.

— Edwards-curve DSA over Curve25519. Deterministic signatures by design (no secret nonce). Fast, small signatures (64 bytes), small public keys (32 bytes), resistant to side-channel attacks. Default in modern libsodium, SSH (ed25519 host keys), and TLS 1.3's signature suite. The recommended choice for new systems.

runs.text: Signatures sign a
hash

of the message, not the message itself (for practical length reasons). The hash function is part of the algorithm specification: Ed25519 uses SHA-512 internally. Never use MD5 or SHA-1 in signature schemes — both have known collision attacks that can enable signature forgery.

RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signatures (not PSS) are still common in legacy TLS stacks and JWTs (RS256). They are not catastrophically broken but are theoretically weaker. When you control both ends, prefer RSA-PSS (PS256/PS384/PS512 in JWT) or switch to Ed25519 entirely.

A digital signature is a proof that the private key holder created or endorsed a message. Anyone with the public key can verify it, but only the private key can produce it. Ed25519 is the clean modern choice; ECDSA works but will break catastrophically if you reuse the signing nonce.

cards.title: TLS 1.3: Handshake, 0-RTT, and What Changed from 1.2
cards.teaser: TLS 1.3 is a near-complete redesign of the protocol, eliminating decade-old vulnerabilities and cutting handshake latency. Developers integrating TLS services need to understand the handshake structure, the 0-RTT trade-off, and which TLS 1.2 features were removed and why.

runs.text: TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, published 2018) removed more than it added, eliminating the mechanism behind BEAST, POODLE, DROWN, LOGJAM, and FREAK in one stroke. The handshake was redesigned from scratch.
TLS 1.3 handshake (simplified):

items.text: ClientHello
— client sends supported cipher suites and key shares for supported groups (Curve25519, P-256). Handshake starts immediately — the client sends its key share before the server responds.
ServerHello + encrypted extensions
— server selects a cipher suite, provides its key share, and immediately encrypts everything after ServerHello. In TLS 1.2, much of this was in plaintext.
Certificate + CertificateVerify + Finished
— server authenticates itself; the Finished message authenticates the entire handshake transcript.
Application data
— begins after 1 round trip (1-RTT). TLS 1.2 required 2 RTT.

runs.text: What TLS 1.3 removed from TLS 1.2:

items.text: RSA key exchange
— eliminated. Static RSA key exchange did not provide forward secrecy; all past traffic can be decrypted if the server's private key is later compromised. TLS 1.3 requires ephemeral Diffie-Hellman.
CBC cipher suites
— eliminated. Only AEAD cipher suites remain: AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305.
SHA-1 and MD5 in signatures
— eliminated.
Compression
— eliminated (was the mechanism behind CRIME attack).

runs.text: 0-RTT (Zero Round Trip Time) resumption allows a client to send application data in the very first message when resuming a previous session. The trade-off: 0-RTT data lacks replay protection. An attacker who captures a 0-RTT request can replay it. Only use 0-RTT for idempotent, replay-safe requests (like GET requests for static content) — never for state-changing operations.

If your service still accepts TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 connections, disable them. Both are formally deprecated (RFC 8996, 2021). TLS 1.2 is acceptable with a carefully restricted cipher list; TLS 1.3 should be the floor for new services. PCI DSS 3.2 required disabling TLS 1.0 by June 2018.

TLS 1.3 cuts the connection setup to one round trip, encrypts more of the handshake, and strips out every broken cipher suite and key exchange method from 1.2. The only trade-off worth knowing: 0-RTT resumption is faster but replay-vulnerable — only use it for safe, idempotent requests.

cards.title: Forward Secrecy and Ephemeral Key Exchange
cards.teaser: Forward secrecy guarantees that capturing and storing today's TLS traffic cannot be decrypted later, even if the server's long-term private key is stolen tomorrow. It is achieved through ephemeral key exchange (ECDHE) and is mandatory in TLS 1.3.

runs.text: The threat forward secrecy defends against: a nation-state or sophisticated attacker records encrypted traffic today and waits. When the target server's private key is eventually compromised (disclosed, stolen, subpoenaed, or cracked), all recorded traffic can be retroactively decrypted — unless forward secrecy was in use.

In TLS without forward secrecy (pre-1.3 RSA key exchange), the server's private key is used to decrypt the client's key exchange message — the session key. Compromise the private key, decrypt any recorded session.
Forward secrecy uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman:

items.text: Both client and server generate fresh (ephemeral) key pairs for each TLS session.
They exchange public halves and derive a shared session key (ECDHE — Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral).
The ephemeral private keys are immediately discarded after the handshake.
The server's long-term private key is used only to sign the ephemeral public key, proving identity. It does not participate in key derivation.

runs.text: Consequence: even if the server's private key leaks, an attacker with a recording of past sessions cannot decrypt them — the ephemeral keys that produced the session key were deleted and cannot be reconstructed.
TLS 1.3 mandates forward secrecy — RSA static key exchange is removed from the specification. In TLS 1.2, you must explicitly configure only cipher suites with
ECDHE
or
DHE
in the name to ensure forward secrecy.

"Harvest now, decrypt later" (HNDL) attacks are a primary motivation for post-quantum cryptography migration. Forward secrecy protects against classical key compromise but not against a future quantum computer that can break ECDHE retroactively. This is why the post-quantum migration is urgent even before quantum computers capable of attacking RSA/ECC exist.

Forward secrecy means each TLS session uses fresh, throwaway keys. Even if your server's private key is stolen years from now, recordings of today's traffic stay encrypted — the throwaway keys used to protect them are long gone.

cards.title: Certificate Transparency: Public Logs for TLS Certificates
cards.teaser: Certificate Transparency (CT) is a public, append-only log of all TLS certificates issued by every participating Certificate Authority. It makes misissued certificates — whether accidental or malicious — publicly detectable within hours of issuance. CT is now required by Chrome and Safari.

runs.text: The CA (Certificate Authority) model for TLS has a fundamental weakness: any one of the hundreds of trusted CAs can issue a certificate for any domain. In 2011, DigiNotar was compromised and issued fraudulent certificates for google.com, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks on Iranian users. The CA had no way to detect the misissued certificates until they were caught in the wild.
Certificate Transparency (RFC 6962, Ben Laurie at Google, 2013) solves the detection problem:

items.text: CAs must submit every issued certificate to one or more public CT logs before the certificate can be trusted.
CT logs are append-only, cryptographically verified Merkle trees. A certificate cannot be retroactively removed or silently altered.
The log returns a Signed Certificate Timestamp (SCT) that the CA embeds in the certificate or delivers via TLS stapling.
Browsers verify that a valid SCT is present before trusting a certificate. Chrome has required CT since 2018; Safari since 2021.

runs.text: What this means for developers and operators:

items.text: Monitor CT logs for your domains.

Tools like crt.sh, Facebook's Certificate Transparency Monitor, and Cloudflare's Certificate Transparency Alerts notify you when a certificate is issued for your domain — even by a CA you didn't use. This is how you detect malicious misissued certificates.
Internal PKI certificates do not appear in public CT logs.
Self-signed or internally-signed certificates bypass CT. For internal service TLS, this is fine — but the CA must be private and not trusted by public browsers.

runs.text: crt.sh (operated by Sectigo) is a free public search interface over CT log data. Searching for your domain shows every certificate ever issued for it, including subdomain certificates. Run this audit for any domain you own — the results are often surprising.

Certificate Transparency is a public noticeboard where every CA must announce every TLS certificate it issues. Browsers check the noticeboard; you can too. If someone gets a fraudulent certificate for your domain, you'll see it within minutes of issuance.

cards.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography: The Migration Ahead
cards.teaser: Quantum computers running Shor's algorithm will break RSA, ECDSA, and ECDHE when they reach sufficient scale — rendering today's public-key infrastructure obsolete. NIST standardized its first post-quantum algorithms in 2024. The migration is already overdue for data with long secrecy requirements.

runs.text: The cryptographic algorithms underlying today's PKI — RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and Elliptic Curve — derive their security from mathematical problems (factoring, discrete logarithm) that classical computers cannot solve at practical key sizes. Shor's algorithm, running on a sufficiently powerful quantum computer, solves both in polynomial time.
The threat timeline has two components:

items.text: "Harvest now, decrypt later" (HNDL)

— adversaries are recording encrypted traffic today. If quantum computers capable of breaking RSA/ECC emerge in 10-15 years, all harvested traffic becomes decryptable. Systems with data that must stay confidential beyond that window need post-quantum migration now.
Key exchange is the most urgent target.
ECDHE, which provides forward secrecy in TLS, is broken by Shor's algorithm. Signatures are less urgent (you only need to forge them at the moment of attack, not retroactively).

runs.text: NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography standardization (finalized 2024):

items.text: ML-KEM (formerly Kyber, FIPS 203)
— lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism. Replaces ECDHE for key exchange. Already deployed in Chrome (X25519Kyber768Draft00 hybrid) and Cloudflare's TLS stack.
ML-DSA (formerly Dilithium, FIPS 204)
— lattice-based digital signature. Replaces ECDSA/Ed25519 for signatures.
SLH-DSA (formerly SPHINCS+, FIPS 205)
— hash-based signature scheme. Conservative, not lattice-based; useful as a hedge if lattice math is later broken.

runs.text: Current best practice: hybrid schemes that combine a classical algorithm (X25519) with a post-quantum algorithm (ML-KEM). If the post-quantum algorithm is later broken, the classical algorithm provides a security floor; if quantum computers arrive, the PQ algorithm provides the ceiling.

Symmetric cryptography (AES) is far less affected by quantum computers. Grover's algorithm provides a quadratic speedup against symmetric keys, effectively halving key strength — meaning AES-128 drops to ~64-bit security against a quantum adversary. AES-256 retains ~128-bit quantum security. This is another reason to default to AES-256 for new systems.

Future quantum computers will break RSA and elliptic curve crypto by solving the underlying math problems efficiently. NIST finalized replacement algorithms in 2024 — Kyber for key exchange, Dilithium for signatures, both based on lattice math. The migration is already in progress in TLS; start planning for your own systems.

cards.title: Putting It Together: Cryptography Primitives Decision Tree
cards.teaser: Knowing individual primitives is not enough — developers need a mental model for selecting the right combination for each use case: encrypting data at rest, securing an API, hashing passwords, or signing a document. This card maps common problems to their correct cryptographic solution.

runs.text: The most common developer cryptography mistake is not using a broken algorithm — it is reaching for the wrong algorithm for the job. The following decision framework covers the cases that appear repeatedly in web application development.

items.text: Encrypt data at rest (symmetric, single key owner):
AES-256-GCM with a randomly generated 256-bit key and unique 96-bit nonce per encryption. Use a KMS (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault) for key management; do not hardcode keys.
Encrypt data for a recipient (asymmetric, no shared key):

Hybrid encryption — generate a random AES-256-GCM key, encrypt the data with it, then encrypt the AES key with the recipient's RSA-OAEP or X25519 public key. This is what PGP, TLS, and age (the file encryption tool) all do.
Store a password:
Argon2id with a random 16-byte salt per user. Never SHA-256, never bcrypt on new systems.
Authenticate an API request / webhook:
HMAC-SHA256 with a shared secret. Verify with constant-time comparison.
Sign a document or JWT:
Ed25519 (or RSA-PSS if legacy compatibility required).
Verify file integrity (no secret needed):
SHA-256. Publish the hash over an authenticated channel.
Derive a key from a password:
Argon2id or PBKDF2 (FIPS). Never raw SHA-256.
Transport-layer security:
TLS 1.3 with a valid CA certificate. Configure HSTS. Let the TLS library handle cipher selection.

runs.text: A key principle from David Wong's
Real-World Cryptography
: when an existing high-level API solves your problem — libsodium's
crypto_secretbox
for symmetric encryption,
crypto_box
for public-key encryption,
crypto_sign
for signatures — use it. The high-level API encodes correct defaults so you cannot accidentally choose ECB mode or a 64-bit nonce.

If you are using cryptography at the level of raw AES calls, HMAC constructions from primitives, or manual RSA padding, you are probably working at the wrong abstraction layer. A well-designed library exposes operations like "seal a message for recipient" and "open a sealed message" — not "XOR these bytes with this keystream."

Match the tool to the job: AES-GCM for data at rest, Argon2 for passwords, HMAC for request authentication, Ed25519 for signatures, TLS 1.3 for transport. When a high-level library API exists that covers your use case, use that — it makes the correct choice for you.

cards.title: Random Number Generation: Why Entropy Matters
cards.teaser: Every cryptographic operation depends on unpredictable randomness — keys, nonces, salts, session tokens. Using a predictable or weak random number generator breaks cryptographic guarantees entirely, regardless of which algorithm you use. Always use a cryptographically secure PRNG.

runs.text: Cryptographic security is only as strong as the randomness that seeded it. A perfectly implemented AES-256-GCM implementation is trivially broken if the key was generated with a predictable random number generator. This is not a theoretical concern: the Debian OpenSSL RNG bug (2008) made every SSL/SSH key generated on Debian and its derivatives since September 2006 predictable, reducing the 2048-bit RSA key space to fewer than 32,768 possible values.
What to use by language:

items.text: Python:
secrets
module (not
random
secrets.token_bytes(32)
for keys,
secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
for tokens.
JavaScript/Node:
crypto.getRandomValues()
(browser) or
crypto.randomBytes()
(Node). Never
Math.random()
Java:
SecureRandom
, not
Random
Go:
crypto/rand
, not
math/rand

runs.text: All modern OS CSPRNGs (
/dev/urandom
on Linux,
CryptGenRandom
on Windows,
getentropy()
syscall) are suitable entropy sources. The old advice to avoid
/dev/urandom
in favor of
/dev/random
is outdated — on Linux 5.6+, both use the same CSPRNG and
/dev/urandom
does not block after the initial seed.

Never seed a PRNG with a timestamp, a process ID, or any other guessable value. Time-seeded PRNGs are a classic vulnerability: an attacker who knows approximately when a session token was generated can enumerate the entire random space it could have come from.

Cryptography is only as secure as the randomness behind it. Use your language's cryptographic random functions (Python's secrets, Node's crypto.randomBytes, Go's crypto/rand) — never Math.random() or language functions designed for simulations.
